newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: More fleeing Afghans reach western city of Herat.
newsitem.headline: More fleeing Afghans reach western city of Herat.

text.p: Hundreds more Afghans fleeing fighting in northwestern Afghanistan arrived in the western city of Herat on Tuesday, a spokesman for a U.N. refugee agency said.
"There are about 4,000 in Herat now and hundreds are still coming," said Rupert Colville, an Islamabad-based spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

The displaced Afghans, mainly women, children and old people, are among 40,000 to 50,000 thought to have fled fierce fighting between the radical Islamic Taleban militia and its northern opponents along the Murghab river in Badghis province.
The Taleban, who captured Kabul on September 27, have been attacking forces loyal to Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum and former Herat governor Ismail Khan in Badghis.
Both sides have used heavy weapons and air power in the see-saw battles in which several towns have changed hands.
Colville said it had taken a U.N. truck convoy carrying food, blankets and tents two days to cover the 130 km (81 miles) from Herat to Qala-i-Nau, capital of the remote province.
Afghans fleeing their villages were trudging across country for three to five days just to reach the main road, he added.
Three trucks with 7,900 blankets set out from the Pakistani border city of Peshawar on Tuesday for what was likely to be a five-day drive through Kabul and Kandahar to Herat, he said.

Colville said UNHCR staff in Herat had enough supplies to cope with the current influx of displaced for the moment. "But if they keep arriving, stocks will be exhausted soon and then we might have quite a big emergency on our hands," he said.

If the Taleban break through in Badghis, they could advance into Faryab province and threaten Dostum's northern heartland. If they are defeated, Dostum and his allies could threaten Herat, seized by the Taleban in September 1995.
Colville said that U.N. relief officials who visited three hospitals in battered towns north of Kabul found doctors working in appalling conditions without proper medical supplies.

He said the three hospitals, in Charikar, Gulbahar and Rokha, were packed with ill-nourished war-wounded from recent battles between the Taleban and the combined forces of Dostum and ousted government commander Ahmad Shah Masood.

"Surgeons are operating without anaesthetic, without electricity, without nurses and without proper supplies," Colville said, adding that conditions were worst in Rokha, a village just inside Masood's Panjsher Valley stronghold.
The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Assistance to Afghanistan planned to send food, medicine and medical equipment to the three hospitals soon, he said.
